Samson told her, “If anyone binds me with seven fresh bowstrings,{d} still damp and unused, I will lose my strength and be like everyone else.”
Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.

She had men waiting in ambush in the next room. She shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” But he snapped the strings like a flax thread that singes in a flame. His secret remained undiscovered.
Delilah accused Samson, “You made a fool of me and lied to me. Now tell me honestly how you can be tied up.”
He told her, “If anyone ties me firmly with new ropes that have never been used, I will lose my strength and be like everyone else.”
Delilah took fresh ropes and bound him, then screamed, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” The ambushers lay waiting in the next room. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like so much thread.
Delilah complained to Samson, “So far you have mocked me and lied. Say how someone might tie you up.” He said, “Weave the seven braids of my hair into the loom’s fabric.”{e}
She secured it with the pin and shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” He woke up and yanked out the pin, the loom, and the fabric.
Then she said, “How can you claim to love me when your heart is elsewhere? Three times now you have made fun of me, and you still have not revealed what makes you so strong.”
Day after day she nagged him with her pleading until he felt sick enough to die.

So he opened his whole heart to her: “A blade has never been used on my head, since I have been set apart for God as a Nazirite from the day of my birth. Shave my head and my strength will drain away; I will turn weak and become like any ordinary man.”

Delilah saw that he had finally told her everything, so she sent word summoning the Philistine rulers: “Come one more time; he has confided in me completely.” The rulers came to her, carrying the silver.
She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to humble{f} him, and his strength left him.
She shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” Waking from his sleep, he thought, “I will break free as before, with a shake.” He had no idea that Yahweh had abandoned him.
And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground grain in the prison.
But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
The Philistine rulers assembled for a great sacrificial feast to their god Dagon{g} and for rejoicing, saying, “Our god has put Samson, our enemy, in our hands.”
When the crowd saw him, they praised their god: “Our god has put into our power the foe who ravaged our land and killed so many of us!”
When their hearts were merry, they said, “Call Samson, so that he may entertain us.” So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy leading him, “Place my hands on the pillars that support the building, so I can lean on them.”
The building was crowded, full of men and women. Every Philistine ruler was present, and some three thousand more were up on the roof, watching Samson perform.
Samson prayed to Yahweh: “Lord Yahweh, remember me! Give me strength just this one time, God, so that with a single blow I may repay the Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson felt for the two central columns that supported the building. He braced himself against them, one under his right hand and the other under his left.

And Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” Then he bent with all his might, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.

His brothers and his father’s whole house came down, collected him, carried him back, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial place of his father Manoah. For twenty years he had been Israel’s judge.

notes.text: Sorek means “choice vine.” The Septuagint (B text) keeps the Hebrew as a name (Alsorech); the A text reads “the brook of Sorek.”
The meaning of Delilah is uncertain; it may be related to dallah, “hair, threads,” or to dalal, “to be weak, small.”
Probably shekels; 1,100 shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). Hebrew “a thousand and a hundred of silver.”
Or “cords” or “sinews”; Hebrew yetarim, used of bowstrings and tent cords.

The Hebrew here appears to be shorter, perhaps because a scribe’s eye skipped between similar words. The Septuagint has a longer text: “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten them with the pin into the wall, then I shall become weak and be like any other man.” And in verse 14: “And while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web.”
Or “to afflict” or “to subdue.” The Septuagint reads “and she began to humble him”; some scholars read “he began to grow weak.”
Dagon was a grain or storm god worshiped in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Philistia.

verses.text: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.{a}

He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver{b} that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse and also spoke it in my hearing—look, the silver is with me; I took it.” And his mother said, “Blessed be my son by Yahweh.”

He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, “I solemnly dedicate the silver to Yahweh from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. So now I will return it to you.”
When he gave the silver back to her, she took two hundred shekels of it to a silversmith, who fashioned a carved idol and a molten one. These stood in Micah’s house.
This Micah owned a shrine.{c} He had an ephod made, and household idols,{d} and appointed{e} one of his own sons to be his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
There was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, belonging to the Judah clan, who was staying there as a resident foreigner.
He left Bethlehem in Judah to live wherever he could find lodging. On his way he reached Micah’s house in Ephraim’s hill country.
Micah asked him, “Where are you from?” He said, “I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, looking for a place to stay.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver{f} a year and a set of clothes and your food.” So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to live with Micah, and the young man became like a son to him.
Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and he was in the house of Micah.
Micah concluded, “Now I am certain that Yahweh will do me good, since a Levite is my priest.”

notes.text: Micah (here Hebrew Mikayehu, verses 1 and 4; elsewhere Mikah) means “Who is like Yahweh?”
Probably shekels; 1,100 shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). Verse 4’s two hundred pieces weighed about 5 pounds (2.3 kg).
Hebrew “a house of God” (or “of gods”).
Hebrew teraphim, small household idols, perhaps also used in divination.
Hebrew “filled the hand of,” an idiom for installing a priest; also in verse 12.
Probably shekels; ten shekels weighed about 4 ounces (115 grams, g).

verses.text: At that time Israel had no king. And at that time the Danite clan was still seeking a place to settle, because it had not yet received an allotment among Israel’s tribes.

From their clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, the Danites picked five capable men to scout and map the land. Their instructions: “Go, survey the country.” They reached Ephraim’s hill country, arrived at Micah’s house, and spent the night.
Near Micah’s house, the young Levite’s accent gave him away to them. They stopped and asked him, “Who brought you here? What is your business in this place? What is your stake here?”
He explained, “Micah made an arrangement with me. He pays me, and I serve as his priest.”
They said, “Ask God, so we can learn whether our mission will succeed.”
The priest told them, “Go in peace. Yahweh is watching over the mission you are on.”

The five men left and reached Laish. They watched the people living there: they were secure, like the Sidonians, calm and trusting, wanting nothing the earth could supply, and prosperous.{a} They lived far from Sidon, with no ties to anyone.{b}
When the five returned to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, the kinsmen asked, “What did you find out?”
They answered, “Let’s march against them! We saw that land, and it is excellent. Why are you sitting still? Don’t hesitate; go and capture the country.
When you arrive, you will find a trusting people and a wide-open country. God has delivered it to you, a place that lacks nothing the earth can provide.”
So six hundred men of the clan of the Danites, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,
They went up and pitched camp at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. For that reason the spot has been named Mahaneh-dan{c} ever since; it lies west{d} of Kiriath-jearim.
And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah.
The five men who had scouted the Laish region said to their kinsmen, “Did you know that one of these houses holds an ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a cast idol? Think about what to do.”
And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the house of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.
The six hundred Danite men, equipped for battle, stood beside the entrance to the gateway.

The five men who had scouted the land went inside and removed the carved idol, the ephod, the household gods, and the molten idol. Meanwhile the priest was standing by the gateway’s entrance with the six hundred armed warriors.
When these went into Micah’s house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
They told him, “Silence! Cover your mouth with your hand, and come along as our father and priest. Would you rather serve one man’s household as priest, or serve a whole tribe and clan of Israel?”
The priest was delighted. He took the ephod, the idols, and the carved image and joined the Danite company.
Then they turned and left, placing the children, the livestock, and the baggage ahead of them.
They were some distance from Micah’s house when the men living in the neighborhood were rallied, and they caught up with the Danites.
Calling out to the Danites, who looked back at them, they asked Micah, “What is wrong? Why have you brought such a crowd?”
He replied, “You carry off the gods I made, along with my priest, and leave. What do I have left? And you ask me, ‘What’s wrong?’”
The Danites warned him, “Keep your voice down around us, or some hot-tempered men may attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives.”
Then the Danites went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.
They carried off Micah’s handiwork and his priest, and reached Laish, a calm and unsuspecting people. They slaughtered them with swords and burned the town to the ground.

No one came to rescue the city, because it lay a long way from Sidon and had no dealings with outsiders. It was situated in the valley by Beth-rehob. The Danites reconstructed the city and made it their home.
They renamed the town Dan after their ancestor Dan, Israel’s son; its earlier name had been Laish.

And the Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses,{e} he and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.{f}
They kept Micah’s carved image for themselves all the time God’s house stood at Shiloh.

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew of this clause is uncertain.
So the Hebrew and the Septuagint (B text). The A text, followed by some scholars, reads “with Aram” (Syria), a difference of one letter in Hebrew (adam, “anyone,” and aram).
Mahaneh-dan means “camp of Dan.”
Hebrew “behind,” that is, west.

Most manuscripts of the Hebrew text read “Manasseh,” but the letter n (nun) is written above the line, raised or “suspended” between the other letters, the only suspended nun in the Hebrew Bible. Without it the word reads “Moses.” Jewish tradition (Talmud, Bava Batra 109b) explains that the scribes added the nun to spare Moses the shame of a grandson who served as an idolatrous priest, while marking it as an addition. The Septuagint A text and the Latin Vulgate read “Moses”; the B text reads “Manasseh.” Gershom was the son of Moses (Exodus 2:22).

So the Hebrew and the Septuagint. Some scholars, with a slight change of the Hebrew, read “the captivity of the ark” (compare 1 Samuel 4:11, 21–22). The captivity of the land may refer to the Assyrian deportations in 734–732 B.C. or 722 B.C.

verses.text: In those days Israel had no king. A certain Levite was living in a remote corner of Ephraim’s hill country, and from Bethlehem in Judah he took a concubine.
His concubine became angry with him{a} and left, going back to her father’s home in Bethlehem in Judah. She remained there four months.

Her husband set out to follow her and win her over, so she would return. He took along his servant and two donkeys. She brought him into her father’s home, and when the young woman’s father spotted him, he welcomed him gladly.
His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, persuaded him to stay, and he lodged with them for three days, eating, drinking, and sleeping there.
On the fourth morning they got up early and he was ready to leave, but the girl’s father urged his son-in-law, “Refresh yourself with a bite to eat, then you can go.”
The two men sat down together to eat and drink. Then the young woman’s father urged the man, “Won’t you agree to stay the night and enjoy yourself?”
When the man stood to leave, his father-in-law pressed him, and he stayed another night.
On the fifth day he rose at dawn to leave. But the young woman’s father urged him, “Eat something first and wait until the afternoon.” So the two of them dined together.

When the man, his concubine, and his servant stood to go, his wife’s father, the young woman’s father, told him, “Look, evening is coming on and the day is nearly gone. Stay one more night. See, the sun is setting. Spend the night here and enjoy yourself. You can get up early tomorrow, begin your trip, and head home.”
But the man refused to stay another night. He rose and left, and reached a point across from Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). His two saddled donkeys were with him, along with his concubine.
By the time they were close to Jebus, the day was nearly gone, and the servant suggested to his master, “Let’s turn off to this Jebusite town and stay the night there.”
His master answered, “We won’t detour into a foreign city whose inhabitants are not Israelites. We will continue to Gibeah.”
He told his servant, “Let’s try to reach one of these towns and stay the night in Gibeah or Ramah.”
So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin,
and they stopped there to spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and took a seat in the town’s public square, but nobody offered them a home for the night.
Then an old man came along from his work in the fields that evening. He was originally from Ephraim’s hill country and was living in Gibeah, though the townspeople were Benjaminites.
The old man looked up and noticed the traveler in the town square. “Where are you headed?” he asked. “Where did you come from?”

He answered, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah toward a remote corner of Ephraim’s hill country, which is my home. I had gone to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am heading to the house of Yahweh,{b} but nobody has invited me into a home.
We carry our own straw and feed for the donkeys, plus bread and wine for me, for your servant woman, and for the young man traveling with us. We need nothing else.”
The old man replied, “You are welcome. Whatever you require, I will provide. Just don’t sleep out in the open square.”
He led them to his house and fed the donkeys. The travelers bathed their feet, then ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, a gang of the town’s scoundrels{c} ringed the house and hammered on its door. They shouted to the elderly owner, “Send out the man who has come to your house, so that we can have sex with him.”
The owner of the house stepped outside and pleaded with them, “No, my friends, please don’t do such a wicked thing. This man is my guest; don’t commit this outrage.
Here are my daughter, a virgin, and his concubine. Let me send them out. Abuse them and treat them however you like, but do not commit such an atrocity against this man.”
The men refused to heed him. So the man grabbed his concubine and shoved her outside to them. They raped her and tortured her throughout the night until morning, and at first light released her.
And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man’s house where her master was, until it was light.
When her master rose that morning and opened the house door to continue his journey, there lay his concubine at the entrance, her hands stretched out on the threshold.
“Get up,” he told her, “we are leaving.” She did not respond.{d} He loaded her on the donkey and started for home.
Once inside his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her body apart into twelve parts, and sent them to every part of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, “Never has such a deed been done or witnessed since the day Israel left Egypt. Think about it, discuss it, and speak up!”

notes.text: Hebrew “played the harlot against him” (zanah). Some Greek manuscripts read “was angry with him,” perhaps reflecting a different Hebrew verb; the Septuagint (B text) reads “departed from him.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “to my house,” which fits verse 29; the Hebrew may have arisen from a misread abbreviation.
Hebrew beliya‘al, “worthlessness.”
The Septuagint adds “for she was dead.”

verses.text: All Israel, from Dan down to Beersheba and from Gilead too, marched out, and the community gathered as one person before Yahweh at Mizpah.
The leaders of every tribe of Israel took their positions in the gathering of God’s people: four hundred thousand{a} infantrymen carrying swords.
(The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone to Mizpah.) The Israelites demanded, “Explain how this wicked deed came about.”
And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, “I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.
During the night the lords of Gibeah attacked me, surrounding the house. They intended to murder me, and they raped my concubine so savagely that she died.
I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent them across Israel’s whole territory, because they have done a vile and shameful thing in Israel.
Look, you Israelites, all of you, give your advice and counsel here.”
The entire people rose together and swore, “None of us will return to his tent or go back to his home.
But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot,

We will pick one man in ten from all Israel’s tribes, one in a hundred, and one in a thousand, to gather food for the army. Then, once the troops arrive, they will punish Gibeah in Benjamin for the disgraceful crime it committed in Israel.”
So the men of Israel assembled against the town, united as a single body.
The tribes of Israel sent envoys to every clan of Benjamin with this question: “What is this crime committed among you?
Surrender those scoundrels in Gibeah, so that we may execute them and cleanse Israel of this evil.” But the Benjaminites refused to obey their fellow Israelites.
Then the Benjaminites came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites recruited from their towns twenty-six thousand{b} swordsmen, in addition to seven hundred elite troops from Gibeah’s population.
Among all these troops were seven hundred select men who were left-handed;{c} each could sling a stone at a hair’s width and never miss.
The men of Israel, not counting Benjamin, numbered four hundred thousand sword-bearers, every one a seasoned warrior.
The Israelites set out for Bethel and asked God, “Which of us should march first against the Benjaminites?” Yahweh answered, “Judah goes first.”
Then the Israelites rose in the morning and camped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel marched against Benjamin and took positions opposite them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day twenty-two thousand men of the Israelites.
But the Israelite soldiers rallied their courage and again assembled in the same location they had occupied the day before.

The Israelites went and wept in Yahweh’s presence until evening, and they asked Yahweh, “Should we once more march out to battle against our kinsmen the Benjaminites?” Yahweh said, “March against them.”
So the Israelites came near against the Benjaminites the second day.
And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed eighteen thousand men of the Israelites. All these were men who drew the sword.

Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before Yahweh and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before Yahweh.
And the Israelites inquired of Yahweh (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

Phinehas, Eleazar’s son and Aaron’s grandson, served before it in those years). The Israelites asked, “Should we go out to battle against our kinsmen the Benjaminites once more, or give up?” Yahweh replied, “Attack! Tomorrow I will hand them over to you.”
So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.
On the third day the Israelites again marched against the Benjaminites and took up positions facing Gibeah, as they had done before.

The Benjaminites advanced against Israel’s army and were lured away from the town. Just as earlier, they began wounding and killing Israelites along the roads, one leading to Bethel, another toward Gibeah, and in the fields, about thirty Israelites in all.
And the Benjaminites said, “They are defeated before us, as at the first.” But the Israelites said, “Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways.”
All Israel’s men left their positions and formed their line at Baal-tamar,{d} while the ambush force burst from its cover west of Geba.{e}
Ten thousand picked soldiers from throughout Israel advanced on Gibeah, and the fighting was fierce. The Benjaminites had no idea that catastrophe was approaching.
Yahweh gave Israel victory over Benjamin, and on that day Israel killed 25,100 Benjaminite swordsmen.
The Benjaminites realized they were losing. Israel’s soldiers had retreated before them, counting on the troops they had hidden near Gibeah.
The ambushers raced into Gibeah, spread out, and put the entire town to the sword.
The agreed signal between the Israelite army and the hidden troops was a tall column of smoke rising from the town
was the cue for Israel’s troops to turn and fight. Benjamin had started to wound and kill some thirty Israelites. They told themselves, “We are beating them just as in the first battle!”
But when the column of smoke started to climb from the town, the Benjaminites looked back, and the whole town was rising in flames to the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them.
They turned away from the Israelites toward the desert, but the battle caught up with them, and men from the towns cut them down in the middle of the fight.
They encircled the Benjaminites, chased them down, and trampled them from Nohah{f} to a point east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell; all of them were men of valor.
The survivors turned and ran for the desert, to the rock of Rimmon. Along the roads five thousand of them were cut down,{g} and the pursuit pressed on as far as Gidom, where two thousand more fell.
So all who fell that day of Benjamin were twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.
But six hundred men turned and ran into the wilderness to Rimmon’s rock, where they stayed for four months.
The Israelites then went back and attacked the rest of Benjamin, killing the inhabitants of every town, human and animal, everything they came across. They also burned every town they reached.

notes.text: The Hebrew word elef, “thousand,” may in some contexts denote a clan or military unit rather than an exact count; the numbers are given here as written. So throughout this chapter.
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint (B text) reads “twenty-three thousand”; compare verses 35 and 46.
Hebrew “bound in the right hand,” as in 3:15. The Septuagint reads “able to use both hands alike.”
Baal-tamar means “lord of the palm tree.”
Maareh-geba probably means “the open area of Geba (or Gibeah)”; the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint keeps it as a name.
Or “from their resting place”; Hebrew menuhah. The Septuagint reads “from Nua.”
Hebrew “gleaned,” that is, picked off like gleanings.

verses.text: At Mizpah the Israelites had taken an oath: “None of us will marry his daughter to a Benjaminite.”
The people came to Bethel and sat in God’s presence until evening, crying aloud in bitter grief.
They asked, “Why, Yahweh, God of Israel, has this befallen Israel, so that one of our tribes is missing today?”
Early the next day the people got up, built an altar there, and presented burnt offerings and fellowship offerings.

The Israelites asked, “Is there any tribe of Israel that did not join the gathering before Yahweh?” They had taken a binding oath that whoever failed to appear before Yahweh at Mizpah must be put to death.
The Israelites felt sorry for their kinsmen the Benjaminites and said, “Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel.
What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by Yahweh that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?”
They asked, “Which of Israel’s tribes failed to come to Yahweh at Mizpah?” They discovered that nobody from Jabesh-gilead had joined the gathering in the camp.
For when the people were mustered, look, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there.
So the assembly sent twelve thousand of its best soldiers with this command: “Go and kill the people of Jabesh-gilead by the sword, women and children included.
Here is what you must do: put to death every man, and every woman who has had intercourse with a man.”{a}

And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole congregation sent word to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them.
At that point Benjamin returned, and the survivors were given the Jabesh-gilead women who had been left alive. Even so, the women did not suffice.{b}
And the people had compassion on Benjamin because Yahweh had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
Then the elders of the congregation said, “What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?”
And they said, “There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel.
Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters.” For the Israelites had sworn, “Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin.”
Then they remembered, “Yahweh’s annual festival is being held at Shiloh,{c} which is north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.”
And they commanded the Benjaminites, saying, “Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards
and keep watch. When Shiloh’s young women come out to join the dancing, run from the vineyards, grab a wife each from among them, and head for Benjamin’s territory.

If their fathers or brothers come to us with complaints, we will tell them, ‘Be generous and let us keep them, since we did not capture a wife for each of them in the war, and you did not give them away yourselves, or you would now be guilty.’”{d}
The Benjaminites did that. They carried off as many wives as they needed from the dancing women. Then they went home to their own land, rebuilt their towns, and settled in them.
The Israelites dispersed from that place, each man to his own tribe and clan, each to his own allotted land.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

notes.text: The Septuagint adds “but the virgins you shall save alive. And they did so.”
Hebrew “but they did not find enough for them.” The Septuagint reads “and it pleased them so.”

Probably the autumn Festival of Booths (Tabernacles), held at the end of the grape harvest in the seventh month (in September–October); compare the vineyards in verses 20–21. This identification is not certain.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Greek manuscripts differ in this verse.
